claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is in a metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution state.
Elevated-temperature aging accelerates atomic diffusion or elemental mobility.
Diffusion-driven local compositional fluctuations overcome an intermetallic nucleation barrier in the metastable solid solution.
Controlled aging produces fine, homogeneously distributed intermetallic precipitates from the metastable solid solution.
Mg-Ti-Zn alloys can contain Ti2Zn and Mg21Zn25 intermetallic compounds.
Ti2Zn and TiZn16 can provide a shielding effect that limits corrosion-front progression in Mg-Ti-Zn alloys.
Ti and Zn in the matrix, together with uniformly distributed fine intermetallics, promote a protective passivating surface film and high corrosion resistance.
Intermetallic precipitates act as preferential nucleation sites for a stable, coherent oxide layer.
TiO2 is an example of the passivating oxide expected to form in the proposed process.
The intermetallic-assisted oxide layer enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Rapid quenching preserves the metastable solid-solution state.
Rapid quenching inhibits formation of beneficial intermetallic precipitates.
Quenched samples eventually form less effective, inhomogeneous oxide layers and consequently exhibit poorer corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Coarse or non-uniform intermetallics can generate micro-galvanic effects that offset passivation benefits and accelerate localized Mg dissolution.
The initial baseline lacks significant intermetallic phases and has only incipient, non-uniform oxide formation.
Aging near 500 °C or above for hours to days is sufficient to drive the proposed diffusion-controlled transformation.
The applicable service-temperature regime is approximately 500–1100 °C, provided exposure lasts long enough for diffusion-driven transformation.
Ultra-short exposure or extremely high temperatures associated with oxide breakdown can alter the proposed transformation kinetics and passivation behavior.
